messages.body_plain:
Sharing my answers in response to the questions:

1) lavPredict uses centered manifest items.

---------------------------------------------------------------
## centered manifest items
lv_B_fsm_hat_center <- data.frame(
  "visual"=scale(mani_items,center=TRUE,scale=FALSE) %*% t(lv_B_fsm))
lv_r_fsm_hat_center <- data.frame(
  "visual"=scale(mani_items,center=TRUE,scale=FALSE) %*% t(lv_r_fsm))

head(cbind(lv_B,lv_B_fsm_hat_center))
max(abs(lv_B-lv_B_fsm_hat_center[,1]))
head(cbind(lv_r,lv_r_fsm_hat_center))
max(abs(lv_r-lv_r_fsm_hat_center[,1]))
---------------------------------------------------------------

2) The factor scores were incorrectly calculated - the correct calculations are below.

---------------------------------------------------------------
sigma <- fitted(fit)$cov
parest <- lavInspect(fit,what="est")
lambda <- parest$lambda
theta <- parest$theta
psi <- parest$psi

## Bartlett
lv_B_fs <- solve(t(lambda) %*% solve(sigma) %*% lambda)[1,1] *
  (t(lambda) %*% solve(sigma))
rbind(lv_B_fsm,lv_B_fs) #equal

## regression
lv_r_fs <- t(psi) %*% (t(lambda) %*% solve(sigma))
rbind(lv_r_fsm,lv_r_fs) #equal
---------------------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: Longitudinal invariance test with two factors
messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal invariance test with two factors
messages.body_plain:
> Is there any source you could suggest, that describes the basics one needs to do this manually?

I'm working on a paper demonstrating invariance tests for categorical indicators across both groups and occasions.  It's not yet in shape enough to share, but if you email me directly (follow the link under my signature), I can make a note to share it with you when it is ready.

> Now, before when I wanted to compare models I just used chi square difference test:

> anova(fit01, fit03)

That's right.

> would that give me configural invariance?

No, configural invariance is not tested using model comparison.  Comparing a model that constrains measurement parameters to equality to a model that does not (i.e., the configural model) tests the null hypothesis that those constraints hold.

Configural invariance is typically tested by looking at that model's chi-squared test, not a chi-squared difference test.  But that conflates configural invariance with all other ways that the configural model is constrained (i.e., why it has degrees of freedom).  You can use a permutation test to test the null hypothesis of configural invariance, irrespective of whether the model fits perfectly.

http://dx.doi.org/10.1037/met0000152

https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01455/full

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Postdoctoral Researcher, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
UvA web page: http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject_clean: Latent growth model for cohort sequential/accelerated longitudinal design
messages.body_plain:
If you have a true cohort sequential design (with a limited number of cohorts) you can also fit a growth model with a multiple group approach. Each cohort is a separate group, and the loadings on the slope latent variable are different across groups representing different times of measurement.

The presentation here (https://www.psychometrics.cam.ac.uk/uploads/documents/ESRC_RDI_April2011/part-5-measurement-invariance.pdf) provides some examples of this approach using Mplus syntax (though I'm not sure why they constrained the residual variances to equality across time.

messages.subject_clean: Longitudinal invariance test with two factors
messages.body_plain:
If you are looking for longitudinal measurement invariance testing in a MGCFA context with categorical data:
Edossa, A. K., Schroeders, U., Weinert, S., & Artelt, C. (2018). The development of emotional and behavioral self-regulation and their effects on academic achievement in childhood. International Journal of Behavioral Development, 42, 192–202. https://doi.org/10.1177/0165025416687412
Yeah, I know shameless self-citing... but Table 1 summarizes the necessary constraints.

In the course of the revision another more technical paper appeared:
Liu, Y., Millsap, R. E., West, S. G., Tein, J.-Y., Tanaka, R., & Grimm, K. J. (2016). Testing measurement invariance in longitudinal data with ordered-categorical measures. Psychological Methods. doi:10.1037/met0000075
Even though the factor loading invariance step doesn't make sense - in my understanding - since factor loadings and intercepts have to be varied in tandem with categorical data.

Hope this helps, kind regards
Ulrich

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to adapt Millsap & Yun-Tein (2004) and Liu et al. (2017)'s categorical invariance cross-sectional and longitudinal models to my dichotomous longitudinal data. I have adapted a script from Sunthud based on Liu et al.'s paper.

I am wondering if someone can confirm that I have specified the correct configural model below?

I ask because when I run the model below I get that the model has not converged. However, when I restrict the factor loadings to be identical across time, the model converges, and when I add the additional constrain that the residual variances are all equal to 1, then the model also converges, and model fit does not degrade suggesting loading, threshold, and variance invariance.

So, I am wondering if I'm setting up my configural model incorrectly or why it might not converge. I can generate data from my data set to replicate my error to share if my code is correct.

Thanks,
Chris

configural.mod <- "

# define the factor models
# Note, the *.1 refers to Time 1, *.2 to Time 2, and *.3 to time 3.
fac2.1 =~ 1 * q1.1 + q4.1 + q10.1 + q11.1 + q19.1 + q23.1 + q27.1 + q28.1 + q15.1

fac2.2 ~~ fac2.2 + fac2.3
fac2.3 ~~ fac2.3

# latent common factor means
fac2.1 ~ 0

messages.body_plain:
For now (using dev 0.6-1), just adding a cluster=  argument is not
enough. You must adapt your syntax and add a level: 1 and level: 2 section.

For example:

myModel <- '
     level: 1
          fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
     level: 2
          fb =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
'

If you have no model for the between level (level 2), create a saturated
model:

  myModel <- '
     level: 1
          fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3 + y4
     level: 2
          y1 ~~ y2 + y3 + y4
          y2 ~~ y3 + y4
          y3 ~~ y4
'

This will not be needed any longer in a next update of 0.6-1, because
this will be the default behavior.

Yves.

Dear Yves,

Thanks a lot for the reply.
I have tried fitting a sem model with all details specified, but I still run into the same error.

I'm following the steps of Hox to conduct a two-level CFA, with 3 latent variables and 10 items.
Model 1 converges (three-factor model at the within-level + null model at between level)
Model 2 converges as well (three-factor model at within-level + independence model at between level), returning some negative variances though
Model 3 doesn't converge, giving the error "Error in ov.names.l[[g]] : subscript out of bounds"

Also tried specifying a between-level model with a saturated individual-level model (because I think that theoretically, my construct should be seen as a shared between-level construct), but that didn't converge either (giving the same error)

I wonder if there is something wrong with my model specification, or if it could be related to Lavaan 0.6.
I'm happy to send you the syntax and relevant information in case you think this needs further investigation.

Thanks for the help,
Sarah

messages.body_plain:
This works for me:

library(lavaan) # must be a 0.6-1 version

FamIQData <- read.table("FamIQData.dat")
names(FamIQData) <- c("family", "child", "wordlist", "cards",
"matrices", "figures", "animals", "occupats")

model1 <- '
   level: 1
     numeric    =~ wordlist + cards + matrices
     perception =~ figures + animals + occupats
   level: 2
     wordlist ~~ 0*wordlist
     cards    ~~ 0*cards
     matrices ~~ 0*matrices
     figures  ~~ 0*figures
     animals  ~~ 0*animals
     occupats ~~ 0*occupats
'

fit1 <- sem(model1, data = FamIQData, cluster = "family",
             std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit1)

model2 <- '
   level: 1
     numeric    =~ wordlist + cards + matrices
     perception =~ figures + animals + occupats
   level: 2
     wordlist ~~ wordlist
     cards    ~~ cards
     matrices ~~ matrices
     figures  ~~ figures
     animals  ~~ animals
     occupats ~~ occupats
'

fit2 <- sem(model2, data = FamIQData, cluster = "family",
             std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit2)

model3 <- '
   level: 1
     numeric    =~ wordlist + cards + matrices
     perception =~ figures + animals + occupats
   level: 2
     # saturated
     wordlist ~~ cards + matrices + figures + animals + occupats
     cards    ~~ matrices + figures + animals + occupats
     matrices ~~ figures + animals + occupats
     figures  ~~ animals + occupats
     animals  ~~ occupats
'

fit3 <- sem(model3, data = FamIQData, cluster = "family",
             std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit3)

model4a <- '
   level: 1
     numeric    =~ wordlist + cards + matrices
     perception =~ figures + animals + occupats
   level: 2
     general    =~ wordlist + cards + matrices +
                   figures + animals + occupats
'

fit4a <- sem(model4a, data = FamIQData, cluster = "family",
              std.lv <http://std.lv> = TRUE, verbose = FALSE)
summary(fit4a)

If this doesn't work for you, please show us your full R script.

Yves.

On Tue, Apr 3, 2018 at 6:42 AM kmarkus via lavaan <lav...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Nicolas,
> I am not sure that you question has a matter of fact answer because it is a matter of accepted practice which may vary by literature.  Here are some thoughts.
>
> One thing that you could do is to extract the sample means, implied means, and mean residuals.  Plotting the first two against time might make a convincing case, particularly combined with the fact that the linear model does not reach a valid solution.
>
> One thing that I notice is that your variable names begin with 'sqr'.  If that stands for square root (or square) you might consider analyzing the variables without the transformation to see if the non-linearity goes away.
>
> You are somewhat limited by having only four time points.  In future studies, if you can collect more time points, you might consider adding a second slope that has fixed zero loadings up until the time point represented by your 3rd time point and then has a linear slope (piecewise growth) or adding a second slope affecting all time points with loadings equal to the square of the linear loadings (quadratic polynomial growth).  Free loadings are not really testing a specific nonlinear hypothesis but just an unspecific alternative hypothesis to the linear null.
>
> You could try constraining the variances to be non-negative and refitting the linear growth model.  I think that it is fair to say that majority opinion has come down on the side that this is not good general practice because it tends to hide problems with the model.  However, in your situation, it may be a useful follow-up to fitting the model without the non-negativitiy constraints.  It might not converge at all but it if does it may give you a poorly fitting solution that passes basic admissibility tests.
>
> I am not a statistician but it seems to me that the following logic holds.  The inadmissible solution represents the best obtainable fit (assuming you get a consistent solution) for the unconstrained linear growth model.  As such, any admissible solution would have to fit worse.  So, if the nonlinear growth model fits better at a statistically significant level, then it must also fit better than any admissible solution for the linear growth model.  However, it may be helpful to compare the inadmissible solution to an admissible solution with constraints, because you would not accept the inadmissible solution even if it fit well, or within sampling error of the non-linear growth model.  Perhaps others can comment on the behavior of chi-square for inadmissible solutions and the validity of such chi-square difference tests.
>
> Keith

> http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

Below is a description of my model and my code:
Description: I am interested in looking at how anthropocentric land use surrounding a site may influence the site's nutrient patterns, which in return may influence plant traits. I measured individual plant traits at several sites, but also measured site-level characteristics (see below). Because several plants were measured at a single site, site is repeated and should be used as a random effect.

natural (factor for either low or high natural land use surrounding the site)
impervious (factor for either low or high amounts of impervious surface surrounding the site)
cv.precipitation (numeric variable for variation in precipitation at the site level)
n_i (factor for whether the surveyed species was native or invasive)

Multiple numeric trait measures
Model:
forb.model<-'
     landuse=~natural+impervious+cv.precipitation

     traits=~avg.height+avg.culms+avg.chloro+avg.sla

     nutrients~traits
'
